title: I shipped a native iOS runner in 7 days with Claude Code — prototype speed was not the bottleneck
author: bespaloff
selftext:
I used a seven-day vacation to build Vibecoder Simulator, a native iOS three-lane runner about vibe coding. Most of the implementation happened through Claude remote sessions that I dictated into from my phone.

  
The first playable prototype arrived very quickly. Finishing something coherent was the hard part.

  
The shipped game is SwiftUI rather than SpriteKit. The runner is drawn in a custom Canvas, the levels are JSON-driven, and most state uses Swift Observation. Players choose Go, SQL, JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, Kotlin, Rust, or Memes; the tokens, code fragments, quizzes, bugs, and bosses change with that choice.

  
Claude Code handled most of the implementation. SpriteCook produced the character and boss sprites. I also used Meshy and Tripo for 3D experiments, Suno for the music, and ElevenLabs for sound effects.

  
I initially tried to turn the runner into a 3D game. The agent could generate plausible code for loading models and moving a camera, but the assets never felt like one world. Scale, materials, animation, framing, and collisions all disagreed with one another. Blender gave me clean geometry, but it also exposed the difference between generating an asset and directing a game. I eventually returned to 2D sprites because that was the visual language I could consistently tune in the time available.

  
The most useful workflow lesson was to report one failure at a time. When I gave Claude five problems in one prompt, I usually got five confident half-solutions. When I said, “The quiz starts before the player can read the briefing; fix only that,” the iteration became predictable. I went through roughly 50 play-test loops like this.

  
AI was excellent at making a rough system exist. Human judgment remained the bottleneck: deciding which jokes were worth interrupting the run, keeping nine selectable tech stacks readable, making levels feel related rather than assembled, and recognizing when an AI-generated asset was technically fine but wrong for the game. Reverting attractive changes that hurt pacing took more discipline than generating new ones.

  
The result is free, works offline, and has no ads or accounts:

[https://apps.apple.com/us/app/vibecoder-simulator/id6803527299](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/vibecoder-simulator/id6803527299)

  
For anyone who has shipped an AI-heavy game: did integration and art direction consume more time than generating the individual pieces? I would also appreciate blunt play-test feedback on where the difficulty stops feeling fair.
